The passage you provided is a critique of Martin Luther, a German theologian and religious reformer, from an unknown author. The passage suggests that Luther's teachings are leading people astray, and it contrasts Luther's path with a righteous one that leads to Elysium (heaven) and away from Tartarus (hell). The passage also mentions the need for virtues such as sobriety, meekness, liberality, well-speaking, modesty, and avoiding wantonness. It also mentions the power of prayer. Here is the passage recited:

"Not endure or turn to the good; they have not the use of oaths, since they neither distrust nor deceive anyone; they know not the hunger for money, since their treasure is in heaven, nor do they itch for empty glory, since they refer all things to the glory of Christ.

You do not agree either with yourself or among yourselves – indeed though you do not even agree with yourself, since in this same Assertion you say one thing in the beginning and something else later on, recanting what you said before. Continuing his chastisement of Luther – and undoubtedly put off by the coming place where cleaves our way in twain. Thy road, the right, toward Pluto's dwelling goes, And leads us to Elysium. But the left Speeds sinful souls to doom, and is their path To Tartarus th' accurst.

Virtue to sobriety, from fury and passion to meekness, from avarice to liberality, from reviling to well-speaking, from wantonness to modesty. I will show you a great many who have become worse through following it. ...The solemn prayers of the saints have more power than all the magic of the sorcerers."
